\begin{abstract}
We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, which compiles Information Extraction (IE) ontology schemas into two composable token-level decoding constraints that enforce structural and type-validity constraints during autoregressive generation:
(1)~a \emph{grammar layer} (XGrammar context-free grammar) guaranteeing JSON structural validity and entity/relation vocabulary membership (virtually eliminating entity type and relation vocabulary violations); and
(2)~a \emph{semantic layer} that enforces per-triple domain/range type constraints via a stateful entity registry and dynamic logit masking, with grammar-first fallback when constraints conflict.
%
Without constraints, Large Language Model (LLM) based IE produces systematic domain/range (DR) violations: 15.37\% on SciERC (7 relations) and 18.46\% on DocRED (96 relations), with 1--2\% persisting even after fine-tuning; rates are driven by \emph{constraint tightness} rather than ontology scale.
Composed with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning, \textsc{OntoCoDec} reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.20\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp of unconstrained baselines (R-F1 40--46), demonstrating near-lossless composability at deployment-grade extraction quality.
% exp_ids: w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval
Under zero-shot decoding, which stress-tests constraint robustness at low extraction quality (R-F1 2--8\%), DR drops by 42--99\% across three model families (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) with no significant F1 cost (DocRED: $+$0.50\,pp, $p{<}0.001$; \S\ref{sec:cross-model}).
With beam search ($k{=}4$), the full stack eliminates all four violation types under fine-tuned beam decoding (SciERC, both Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B) while preserving extraction quality (R-F1 44.23 and 46.11, respectively); in zero-shot beam decoding, DR reaches 0\% for calibrated models on both RE datasets.
The framework generalizes to event extraction (WikiEvents: 56 event types, 80 roles) without architectural modification and eliminates event-vocabulary and role-vocabulary violations ($\to$ 0\%); where unconstrained outputs are severely off-schema, format compliance additionally enables entity extraction (Entity F1: 0\%\,$\to$\,12--18\%).
Per-slot enforcement introduces a cross-field consistency trade-off (up to 12\% in zero-shot, resolved to $\leq$1.2\% by fine-tuning).
OntoCoDec demonstrates that ontology schemas can be compiled into decoding-time constraints that compose losslessly with standard fine-tuning, bridging the gap between flexible generative extraction and the type-safety requirements of downstream knowledge systems.
\end{abstract}

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity is guaranteed to carry a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 1--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning, driven by \emph{constraint tightness} (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology scale.
Constraint enforcement matters most at deployment-grade quality (R-F1 40--46\%): at this level, residual type violations propagate directly into knowledge graphs and decision-support pipelines; reliable type-safety enforcement is needed.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} guarantees syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in most zero-shot settings via precision gains, but at the cost of discarding up to 48\% of predictions including true positives; at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it discards the majority of outputs, making it impractical.
OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation rather than discarding non-compliant outputs.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} provide only soft guidance that cannot eliminate violations.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec} (\textbf{Onto}logy-\textbf{Co}mpiled \textbf{Dec}oding), a framework that compiles an IE ontology into two composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
Our two-layer architecture reflects the observation that structural violations (malformed output, unknown types) and semantic violations (type-constraint breaches) require fundamentally different enforcement mechanisms.
The \emph{grammar layer} enforces JSON well-formedness and vocabulary validity via XGrammar.
The \emph{semantic layer} maintains a stateful entity registry during generation: as entities are decoded, the registry records type assignments; when relation arguments are generated, dynamic logit masking restricts output to types compatible with the relation's domain/range specification.
The layers compose via bitwise AND with an \emph{enabling dependency}: the grammar layer guarantees vocabulary membership, so the semantic layer can look up domain/range rules.
Unlike type-constrained code generation where types are statically declared, IE requires a dynamic entity registry built during generation, with constraint targets that depend on the co-occurring relation.
Composed with LoRA fine-tuning, OntoCoDec reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.20\% at $<$0.6\,pp F1 cost (R-F1 40--46); under zero-shot decoding (R-F1 2--8\%), which stress-tests constraint robustness, DR drops by 94\% on SciERC while remaining F1-neutral.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The first systematic study of ontological constraint violations in LLM-based IE (spanning per-relation tightness analysis, dual-factor characterization, and post-hoc baseline comparison), violation rates are driven by constraint tightness rather than ontology size, and prompt-level intervention is per-relation unreliable.
    \item OntoCoDec, a two-layer compiled constraint framework that is the first to enforce pair-based domain/range type constraints via compiled stateful logit masks during autoregressive IE.
    Unlike type-constrained decoding in code generation, where output types are statically determined by the grammar, IE requires stateful cross-field constraints because entity type validity depends on the co-occurring relation within each triple.
    \item Near-lossless composability with LoRA fine-tuning: DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% at $<$0.6\,pp F1 cost (R-F1 40--46) on 2 models $\times$ 2 datasets; zero-shot stress test on 3 models $\times$ 3 datasets (2 RE + 1 EE) confirms robustness: DR $\downarrow$76--99\% on SciERC, $\downarrow$42--90\% on DocRED with significant R-F1 gains (Qwen $p{<}0.001$, Llama $p{=}0.013$); cross-task generalization to WikiEvents (vocabulary violations $\to$\,0\%; Entity F1 0\%\,$\to$\,12--18\%).
    \item Characterization of the CF$\leftrightarrow$DR trade-off inherent in per-slot enforcement (resolved by fine-tuning to CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\%); beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all four violation types under fine-tuned beam decoding (SciERC, both Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B) and reduces DR to 0\% for calibrated models in zero-shot settings.
\end{enumerate}

37	\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
38	The composition framework scales from worst-case to deployment settings.
39	Fine-tuning narrows the fallback regime: DR drops from 0.93--10.21\% (zero-shot) to $\leq$\,0.20\% (LoRA), and CF from 2.57--9.90\% to $\leq$\,1.18\%, while R-F1 remains within $\pm$0.6\,pp.

42	\paragraph{Decidability Taxonomy.}
43	We classify constraints by when sufficient information becomes available: \emph{local} (current token only, e.g., vocabulary membership; grammar layer), \emph{prefix-decidable} (decoded prefix, e.g., domain/range; semantic layer), and \emph{non-local} (forward coreference; outside single-pass decoding, partially addressed by S2, \S\ref{sec:s2}).

% Section: Constraint Composition (compressed, 787→~500 words)

At each decoding step $t$, let $G(t) \subseteq V$ and $S(t) \subseteq V$ denote the tokens permitted by the grammar and semantic layers, respectively.
The final mask is their conjunction:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
\end{equation}
%
so a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
The conjunction is asymmetric: $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$, reflecting the enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:method}): the semantic layer requires the relation type to belong to $\mathcal{R}$, a property guaranteed only by the grammar layer.

\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ (tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid), na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: if no semantically valid token survives grammar filtering, semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.
Structural integrity is a hard constraint; a type violation is a soft error detectable by downstream validation.

\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}
We define the tightness of relation $r$ as:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tightness}
  \kappa(r) = 1 - \frac{|\mathcal{V}(r)|}{|\mathcal{E}|^2},
\end{equation}
%
where $\mathcal{V}(r)$ is the set of valid type pairs and $\mathcal{E}$ the entity type vocabulary.
The mean tightness $\bar{\kappa} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r} \kappa(r)$ characterizes ontology restrictiveness.
Tighter constraints eliminate more grammar-valid tokens at type-bearing positions, increasing fallback frequency and residual DR.
This dual-factor pattern (tightness $\times$ baseline model violation rate) is consistent with the cross-dataset results: for calibrated models (Qwen, Llama), SciERC ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$, 24 valid pairs/relation) achieves 94--99\% DR reduction, while DocRED ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$, 5.68 pairs) achieves 45--90\%; including Mistral (whose high baseline ET shifts the regime), the full range across all three models is 42--99\% (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}; quantitative analysis in Appendix~\ref{app:dual-factor}).
This pattern is observed across four model-dataset configurations; additional settings would be needed to establish statistical robustness.

\paragraph{Non-Rectangularity and Sequential Masking.}
\label{sec:rectangularity}
% Data source: artifacts/rebuttal/w2_rectangularity_report.md
Sequential masking ($\tau^h \in \operatorname{dom}(r)$, then $\tau^t \in \operatorname{range}(r, \tau^h)$) is necessary because real ontology type signatures are non-rectangular: 0/7 SciERC and only 23/96 DocRED relations satisfy $\sigma(r) = \operatorname{dom}(r) \times \operatorname{range}(r)$.
Independent enforcement would admit 33--37\% spurious type pairs; on SciERC, 100\% of residual DR under S1 are pairs that pass independent checks but violate $\sigma(r)$.

\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
The composition framework scales from worst-case to deployment settings.
Fine-tuning narrows the fallback regime: DR drops from 0.93--10.21\% (zero-shot) to $\leq$\,0.20\% (LoRA), and CF from 2.57--9.90\% to $\leq$\,1.18\%, while R-F1 remains within $\pm$0.6\,pp.
This confirms the enabling dependency's practical payoff: under fine-tuning, the grammar layer becomes a no-op (models produce valid vocabulary), and the semantic layer alone reduces residual DR by 39--72\% (\S\ref{sec:composability}).

% Section 3 — Method (Draft)
% OntoCoDec: Type-Valid Information Extraction
% via Compiled Ontology Constraints

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

We present OntoCoDec, a two-layer constrained decoding framework that compiles ontology schemas into token-level masks enforced during autoregressive generation.
Unlike type-constrained code generation, IE presents three distinct challenges: (1)~entity types are inferred from free text rather than declared annotations, (2)~the entity registry is built dynamically during generation, and (3)~constraint targets are context-dependent type assignments rather than fixed grammar productions.
The grammar layer (\S\ref{sec:grammar}) guarantees structural validity (well-formed JSON with ontology-vocabulary membership), while the semantic layer (\S\ref{sec:semantic}) enforces domain/range type constraints via a stateful entity registry.
We describe the problem formulation (\S\ref{sec:formulation}), each layer, and two decoding strategies (\S\ref{sec:strategies}).
Formal analysis of constraint composition is deferred to Section~\ref{sec:composition}.


\subsection{Problem Formulation}

\label{sec:violation_landscape}

\paragraph{Setup.}
We evaluate on two IE benchmarks:
\textbf{SciERC}~\cite{luan2018scierc} (551 test sentences, 7 relations, avg.\ 26.1 valid type pairs/relation) and \textbf{DocRED}~\cite{yao2019docred} (998 dev documents,\footnote{DocRED test annotations are not publicly available; we evaluate on the development set.} 96 relations, avg.\ 5.68 valid pairs).
Primary model: Qwen3-8B~\cite{qwen2025qwen3}, zero-shot greedy decoding; cross-model validation in \S\ref{sec:cross-model}.
We measure four violation categories: \textbf{DR} (domain/range type pair $\notin \sigma(r)$), \textbf{RV} (relation $\notin \mathcal{R}$), \textbf{ET} (entity type $\notin \mathcal{E}$), and \textbf{CF} (same entity assigned conflicting types across triples).
Violation rates are computed over successfully parsed documents; including failures as zero-violation instances adjusts rates by at most 0.23\,pp.

\paragraph{Baseline violations and motivation.}
DR violations affect 15.37\% of triples on SciERC and 18.46\% on DocRED, comparable rates despite 14$\times$ ontology size difference; severity is driven by \emph{constraint tightness} rather than scale.
Per-relation rates vary by over 40\,pp (Appendix~\ref{app:per-relation-landscape}), correlating with tightness $\kappa(r)$.
RV on DocRED reaches 29.66\%: large vocabularies exceed prompt-based reproduction capacity.
Schema-informed prompting reduces DR by 62\% on SciERC but only 30\% on DocRED and is per-relation unreliable (DR for \textsc{Evaluate-for} \emph{increases} by 5.8\,pp). These limitations motivate decoding-time enforcement.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   The user is the Director of an ML research project (`schema_semantic_constrained_ie`), directing a Paper Agent to perform structural revisions on an EMNLP 2026 paper titled "OntoCoDec: Type-Constrained Information Extraction via Compiled Ontology Constraints." The overarching goal is implementing the D057 revision plan based on Dream simulation feedback (three tiers of reviewers all scored 3.5). The revisions include:
   - **Task 1 (DONE)**: Fix "formal guarantee" wording — grammar layer can say "guarantee", semantic layer must say "enforce with graceful degradation", system-level cannot use "guarantee"
   - **Task 2 (DONE)**: Major narrative reframe from zero-shot → fine-tuned as primary story (the most critical change)
   - **Task 3 (DONE)**: Decidability taxonomy downgraded from standalone contribution to design motivation (Option A)
   - **Task 4 (IN PROGRESS)**: Full narrative consistency audit across all sections
   - **Task 5 (PENDING)**: Beam+FT positioning as "crown jewel" evidence
   
   Additional completed tasks: BibTeX consistency check, latency data update (P8b DocRED), EnriCo+IterGen comparison paragraphs.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **OntoCoDec**: Two-layer constrained decoding framework (grammar layer + semantic layer)
   - **Grammar layer**: Guarantees JSON structural validity + vocabulary membership via XGrammar (CFG)
   - **Semantic layer**: Enforces domain/range type constraints via stateful entity registry + dynamic logit masking, with grammar-first fallback
   - **Constraint tightness** (κ): Metric determining violation rates; SciERC κ̄=0.333, DocRED κ̄=0.842
   - **DR/RV/ET/CF violations**: Four violation categories (domain/range, relation vocabulary, entity type, cross-field consistency)
   - **Fine-tuned composability**: LoRA + OntoCoDec = DR≤0.20%, R-F1±0.6pp, CF≤1.18%
   - **Zero-shot as "stress test"**: R-F1 2-8%, proves robustness under worst-case conditions
   - **Beam search (k=4) + LoRA**: Eliminates ALL four violation types (crown jewel result)

% Section: Constraint Composition (compressed, 787→~500 words)

At each decoding step $t$, let $G(t) \subseteq V$ and $S(t) \subseteq V$ denote the tokens permitted by the grammar and semantic layers, respectively.
The final mask is their conjunction:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
\end{equation}
%
so a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
The conjunction is asymmetric: $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$, reflecting the enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:method}): the semantic layer requires the relation type to belong to $\mathcal{R}$, a property guaranteed only by the grammar layer.

\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ (tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid), na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: if no semantically valid token survives grammar filtering, semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.
Structural integrity is a hard constraint; a type violation is a soft error detectable by downstream validation.

\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}
We define the tightness of relation $r$ as:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tightness}
  \kappa(r) = 1 - \frac{|\mathcal{V}(r)|}{|\mathcal{E}|^2},
\end{equation}
%
where $\mathcal{V}(r)$ is the set of valid type pairs and $\mathcal{E}$ the entity type vocabulary.
The mean tightness $\bar{\kappa} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r} \kappa(r)$ characterizes ontology restrictiveness.
Tighter constraints eliminate more grammar-valid tokens at type-bearing positions, increasing fallback frequency and residual DR.
This dual-factor pattern (tightness $\times$ baseline model violation rate) is consistent with the cross-dataset results: for calibrated models (Qwen, Llama), SciERC ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$, 24 valid pairs/relation) achieves 94--99\% DR reduction, while DocRED ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$, 5.68 pairs) achieves 45--90\%; including Mistral (whose high baseline ET shifts the regime), the full range across all three models is 42--99\% (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}; quantitative analysis in Appendix~\ref{app:dual-factor}).
This pattern is observed across four model-dataset configurations; additional settings would be needed to establish statistical robustness.

\paragraph{Non-Rectangularity and Sequential Masking.}
\label{sec:rectangularity}
% Data source: artifacts/rebuttal/w2_rectangularity_report.md
Sequential masking ($\tau^h \in \operatorname{dom}(r)$, then $\tau^t \in \operatorname{range}(r, \tau^h)$) is necessary because real ontology type signatures are non-rectangular: 0/7 SciERC and only 23/96 DocRED relations satisfy $\sigma(r) = \operatorname{dom}(r) \times \operatorname{range}(r)$.
Independent enforcement would admit 33--37\% spurious type pairs; on SciERC, 100\% of residual DR under S1 are pairs that pass independent checks but violate $\sigma(r)$.

\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
The composition framework scales from worst-case to deployment settings.
Fine-tuning narrows the fallback regime: DR drops from 0.93--10.21\% (zero-shot) to $\leq$\,0.20\% (LoRA), and CF from 2.57--9.90\% to $\leq$\,1.18\%, while R-F1 remains within $\pm$0.6\,pp.
This confirms the enabling dependency's practical payoff: under fine-tuning, the grammar layer becomes a no-op (models produce valid vocabulary), and the semantic layer alone reduces residual DR by 39--72\% (\S\ref{sec:composability}).

The two-layer design reflects when constraint information becomes available during decoding: vocabulary membership is decidable from the current token (grammar layer), while domain/range requires the decoded prefix (semantic layer, \S\ref{sec:semantic}); forward coreference remains outside single-pass decoding, partially addressed by S2 (\S\ref{sec:s2}).

% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion (maximally compressed)
% Full discussion in Appendix; Mistral boundary condition in app:dual-factor.

OntoCoDec compiles IE ontology schemas into composable token-level decoding constraints that compose losslessly with standard fine-tuning: DR reaches $\leq$\,0.20\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp (R-F1 40--46), and beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all four violation types for calibrated models (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
Under zero-shot decoding, which stress-tests constraint robustness at R-F1 2--8\%, DR drops by 42--99\% across three models $\times$ three datasets with no significant F1 cost, confirming effectiveness across the full quality spectrum.
CF remains an open challenge for per-slot enforcement; global entity-level type consensus during decoding offers the most direct resolution path.

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity is guaranteed to carry a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 1--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning, driven by \emph{constraint tightness} (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology scale.
Constraint enforcement matters most at deployment-grade quality (R-F1 40--46\%): at this level, residual type violations propagate directly into knowledge graphs and decision-support pipelines; reliable type-safety enforcement is needed.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} guarantees syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in most zero-shot settings via precision gains, but at the cost of discarding up to 48\% of predictions including true positives; at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it discards the majority of outputs, making it impractical.
OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation rather than discarding non-compliant outputs.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} provide only soft guidance that cannot eliminate violations.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec} (\textbf{Onto}logy-\textbf{Co}mpiled \textbf{Dec}oding), a framework that compiles an IE ontology into two composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
Our two-layer architecture reflects the observation that structural violations (malformed output, unknown types) and semantic violations (type-constraint breaches) require fundamentally different enforcement mechanisms.
The \emph{grammar layer} enforces JSON well-formedness and vocabulary validity via XGrammar.
The \emph{semantic layer} maintains a stateful entity registry during generation: as entities are decoded, the registry records type assignments; when relation arguments are generated, dynamic logit masking restricts output to types compatible with the relation's domain/range specification.
The layers compose via bitwise AND with an \emph{enabling dependency}: the grammar layer guarantees vocabulary membership, so the semantic layer can look up domain/range rules.
Unlike type-constrained code generation where types are statically declared, IE requires a dynamic entity registry built during generation, with constraint targets that depend on the co-occurring relation.
Composed with LoRA fine-tuning, OntoCoDec reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.20\% at $<$0.6\,pp F1 cost (R-F1 40--46); under zero-shot decoding (R-F1 2--8\%), which stress-tests constraint robustness, DR drops by 94\% on SciERC while remaining F1-neutral.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The first systematic study of ontological constraint violations in LLM-based IE (spanning per-relation tightness analysis, dual-factor characterization, and post-hoc baseline comparison), violation rates are driven by constraint tightness rather than ontology size, and prompt-level intervention is per-relation unreliable.
    \item OntoCoDec, a two-layer compiled constraint framework that is the first to enforce pair-based domain/range type constraints via compiled stateful logit masks during autoregressive IE.
    Unlike type-constrained decoding in code generation, where output types are statically determined by the grammar, IE requires stateful cross-field constraints because entity type validity depends on the co-occurring relation within each triple.
    \item Near-lossless composability with LoRA fine-tuning: DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% at $<$0.6\,pp F1 cost (R-F1 40--46) on 2 models $\times$ 2 datasets; zero-shot stress test on 3 models $\times$ 3 datasets (2 RE + 1 EE) confirms robustness: DR $\downarrow$76--99\% on SciERC, $\downarrow$42--90\% on DocRED with significant R-F1 gains (Qwen $p{<}0.001$, Llama $p{=}0.013$); cross-task generalization to WikiEvents (vocabulary violations $\to$\,0\%; Entity F1 0\%\,$\to$\,12--18\%).
    \item Characterization of the CF$\leftrightarrow$DR trade-off inherent in per-slot enforcement (resolved by fine-tuning to CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\%); beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all four violation types under fine-tuned beam decoding (SciERC, both Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B) and reduces DR to 0\% for calibrated models in zero-shot settings.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{abstract}

%

Composed with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning, \textsc{OntoCoDec} reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.20\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp of unconstrained baselines (R-F1 40--46), demonstrating near-lossless composability at deployment-grade extraction quality.

\label{sec:violation_landscape}

\paragraph{Setup.}
We evaluate on two IE benchmarks:
\textbf{SciERC}~\cite{luan2018scierc} (551 test sentences, 7 relations, avg.\ 26.1 valid type pairs/relation) and \textbf{DocRED}~\cite{yao2019docred} (998 dev documents,\footnote{DocRED test annotations are not publicly available; we evaluate on the development set.} 96 relations, avg.\ 5.68 valid pairs).
Primary model: Qwen3-8B~\cite{qwen2025qwen3}, zero-shot greedy decoding; cross-model validation in \S\ref{sec:cross-model}.
We measure four violation categories: \textbf{DR} (domain/range type pair $\notin \sigma(r)$), \textbf{RV} (relation $\notin \mathcal{R}$), \textbf{ET} (entity type $\notin \mathcal{E}$), and \textbf{CF} (same entity assigned conflicting types across triples).
Violation rates are computed over successfully parsed documents; including failures as zero-violation instances adjusts rates by at most 0.23\,pp.

\paragraph{Baseline violations and motivation.}
DR violations affect 15.37\% of triples on SciERC and 18.46\% on DocRED, comparable rates despite 14$\times$ ontology size difference; severity is driven by \emph{constraint tightness} rather than scale.
Per-relation rates vary by over 40\,pp (Appendix~\ref{app:per-relation-landscape}), correlating with tightness $\kappa(r)$.
RV on DocRED reaches 29.66\%: large vocabularies exceed prompt-based reproduction capacity.
Schema-informed prompting reduces DR by 62\% on SciERC but only 30\% on DocRED and is per-relation unreliable (DR for \textsc{Evaluate-for} \emph{increases} by 5.8\,pp). These limitations motivate decoding-time enforcement.

%          phase2_scierc_semantic_only, phase2_scierc_full_s1, phase2_scierc_full_s2
% All numbers verified against registry 2026-05-14.

\subsection{Ablation and Composability with Fine-Tuning}
\label{sec:scierc-results}

Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation} presents the five-way ablation on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, zero-shot, 551 documents); only the active constraint layers differ across rows.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  Table: SciERC five-way ablation
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3.6pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}l rrrrr rr@{}}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{5}{c}{\textbf{Violation Rates (\%)}}
& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{F1}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-6} \cmidrule(l){7-8}
\textbf{Mode}
  & DR\,$\downarrow$ & $\Delta$DR
  & RV\,$\downarrow$ & ET\,$\downarrow$ & CF
  & Rel.\,$\uparrow$ & Ent.\,$\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
Unconstrained
  & 15.37 & ---
  & 1.39  & 0.40
  & 0.08
  & 8.23  & 31.01 \\
Grammar
  & 14.84 & $\downarrow$3\%
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 0.08
  & 8.23  & 30.98 \\
Semantic
  & 11.65 & $\downarrow$24\%
  & 1.51  & 0.40
  & 2.71
  & 8.15  & 31.01 \\
Full (S1)
  & \textbf{0.93} & $\downarrow$\textbf{94\%}
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 9.90
  & \textbf{8.36} & 30.98 \\
Full (S2)
  & 0.97  & $\downarrow$94\%
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 8.03
  & 8.03  & \textbf{31.90} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}%
\caption{Five-way ablation on SciERC (551 docs, Qwen3-8B, zero-shot).
$\Delta$DR: relative change vs.\ unconstrained.
Best per column in \textbf{bold} (CF excluded).
F1 $\times$100. Bootstrap: 10{,}000 iterations.}
\label{tab:scierc-ablation}
\end{table}

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (a) Core result
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Zero-shot diagnostic: DR elimination at zero F1 cost.}
Zero-shot decoding stress-tests constraint enforcement at low extraction quality (R-F1 2--8\%).
The full two-layer constraint configuration (S1) reduces domain/range
violations from 15.37\% to 0.93\%, a 94\% relative reduction,
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: DR=0.1537; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093
while relation F1 moves from 8.23 to 8.36 ($+$0.13\,pp; bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$0.24, $+$0.58]\,pp, $p = 0.58$, 10{,}000 iterations).
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: R-F1=0.0823; phase2_scierc_full_s1: R-F1=0.0836
% bootstrap: delta=+0.13pp, CI=[-0.24,+0.58], p=0.5824
The difference is not statistically significant ($p = 0.58$); constraint enforcement is F1-neutral on this dataset.
Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in most zero-shot settings via precision gains from aggressive violation removal (SciERC: 8.63 vs.\ 8.36; DocRED: 9.61 vs.\ 8.23), but at the cost of discarding up to 48\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}); OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation.
Per-relation DR drops to $\leq$2.82\% on all types, reaching 0\% on four of seven (Appendix~\ref{app:per-relation-landscape}).
However, constraint enforcement elevates CF from 0.08\% to 9.90\% (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (b) Grammar layer
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Grammar layer: cost-free structural guarantees.}
Grammar-only constraints eliminate RV (1.39\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and ET (0.40\%\,$\to$\,0\%) with no F1 impact, while DR remains unchanged (15.37\%\,$\to$\,14.84\%).
This configuration represents the capability ceiling of grammar-based constrained decoding~\cite{geng2023gcd}, which enforces JSON structure and vocabulary membership but cannot reason about cross-field semantic constraints.
% phase2_scierc_grammar_only: RV=0, ET=0, DR=0.1484, R-F1=0.0823

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (c) Enabling dependency
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Enabling dependency.}
Semantic-only reduces DR by only 24\% (11.65\%) and cannot eliminate RV (1.51\%) or ET (0.40\%), which establishes the \emph{enabling dependency}: without grammar-enforced vocabulary, the semantic layer encounters OOV types with no domain/range rules.
Adding the grammar layer yields a further 92\% reduction (11.65\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (d) S1 vs S2
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{S1 vs.\ S2.}
S2 achieves comparable DR (0.97\%) but lower R-F1 (8.03 vs.\ 8.36) with fewer triples (1{,}644 vs.\ 1{,}729) and does not resolve the CF trade-off (8.03\% vs.\ 9.90\%); we adopt S1 as the primary configuration.
% phase2_scierc_full_s2: DR=0.0097, R-F1=0.0803, CF=0.0803, triples=1644

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (e) Composability with Fine-Tuning
%  exp_ids: lora_scierc_unconstrained, lora_scierc_full_s1
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}
Table~\ref{tab:composability} tests composability across zero-shot vs.\ LoRA $\times$ unconstrained vs.\ S1 for Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B.
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_full_s1,
%          w5_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval,
%          llama_scierc_unconstrained, llama_scierc_full_s1,
%          w5_llama_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval

Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 1--2\% but leaves residual violations on tight-constraint relations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}).
Adding S1 eliminates these: Qwen DR 1.95\%\,$\to$\,0\% ($-$0.09\,pp R-F1), Llama DR 1.11\%\,$\to$\,0.09\% ($+$0.02\,pp).
On DocRED, the same pattern holds: Qwen DR 0.76\%\,$\to$\,0.01\% ($-$0.30\,pp), Llama DR 0.49\%\,$\to$\,0.20\% ($+$0.51\,pp).
% w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval: DR=0.01%, R-F1=40.56; w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval: DR=0.20%, R-F1=44.23

Across all settings, fine-tuned + S1 yields DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp, which supports orthogonal composability.
Post-fine-tuning, grammar is a no-op; the semantic layer alone reduces DR by 39--72\% (Appendix~\ref{app:ft-ablation}).
CF interference drops from $+$9.82\,pp (zero-shot) to $+$1.18\,pp (fine-tuned), tracing to \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X schema ambiguity (Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}).
Beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates residual DR and reduces CF to $<$1\% for both Qwen and Llama (Appendix~\ref{app:beam-search}).

1	% Appendix B — Extended Discussion
2	% Contains discussion paragraphs moved from the main text during compression.
3	
4	\section{Extended Discussion}\label{app:discussion}
5	
6	%%% CF Dual Mechanism %%%
7	% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1, llama_scierc_full_s1, llama_docred_full_s1
8	
9	\paragraph{CF Dual Mechanism.}
10	CF violations arise from two distinct mechanisms:
11	(1)~\emph{Registry override}: the semantic constraint forces a domain-compatible type that conflicts with the entity's previously registered type.
12	The entity appears in multiple relations with different type requirements, and the per-relation mask selects the locally valid type without consulting prior assignments.
13	(2)~\emph{Grammar-first fallback} (\S\ref{sec:interaction}): when the semantic mask conflicts with all grammar-valid tokens, the semantic layer is dropped entirely, allowing the grammar layer to generate any structurally valid type, which may differ from the entity's registered type.
14	
15	These mechanisms have sharply different model profiles.
16	Qwen3-8B triggers zero grammar-first fallbacks across all experiments, attributing 100\% of its CF violations to registry override.
17	Llama-3.1-8B, by contrast, triggers 5{,}882 fallbacks on SciERC (10.7 per document) and 57{,}825 on DocRED (63.8 per document), making grammar-first fallback the dominant CF source.
18	This asymmetry is consistent with the cross-model CF gap: Qwen achieves CF\,=\,2.57\% on DocRED vs.\ Llama's 12.02\%, despite both using identical constraint configurations.
19	The difference traces to Llama's less calibrated type predictions, which more frequently conflict with the semantic mask's valid set, triggering fallback.
20	
21	%%% Fallback Behavior and Effective Coverage %%%
22	% exp_ids: cf_fallback_ablation_scierc (final data)
23	
24	\paragraph{Fallback Behavior and Effective Coverage.}
25	\label{app:fallback-coverage}
26	The two-layer architecture produces two distinct fallback mechanisms with different semantic consequences.
27	\emph{Grammar-first fallback} (36.6\% of type-bearing positions on SciERC) occurs when $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$: the semantic layer deactivates as a safety valve, preserving structural validity at the cost of potential type violations. These events account for the residual DR that persists after constraint enforcement.
28	\emph{Registry-consistent fallback} (4.5\%) occurs when the entity's registered type conflicts with domain/range constraints; the system defaults to the registered type for cross-triple consistency.
29	Together, these mechanisms produce the characteristic profile of composable constraint systems: residual DR traces to grammar-first fallback events, while CF violations arise from registry override events where per-relation enforcement assigns conflicting types.
30	
31	We define \emph{effective semantic constraint coverage} as $1 - f_{\text{gf}}$, where $f_{\text{gf}}$ is the grammar-first fallback rate.
32	On SciERC, Llama-3.1-8B shows $f_{\text{gf}} = 36.6\%$ (6{,}237 of 17{,}024 mask calls), yielding 63.4\% effective coverage.
33	On DocRED, by contrast, Qwen3-8B shows $f_{\text{gf}} = 0.08\%$ (46 of 54{,}859), yielding 99.9\% coverage.
34	The large discrepancy is primarily a tokenization artifact: SciERC entity types are multi-token (e.g., \textsc{OtherScientificTerm}, averaging 2.87 mask calls per type field), and continuation tokens necessarily conflict with the semantic mask, inflating the per-mask-call fallback rate.
35	DocRED types (\textsc{PER}, \textsc{ORG}, \textsc{LOC}, \textsc{TIME}, \textsc{NUM}, \textsc{MISC}) are all single-token, eliminating this inflation.
36	This metric directly quantifies the enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:interaction}): it measures the fraction of decoding steps where both constraint layers are jointly active, providing a fine-grained view beyond aggregate violation rates.
37	Qwen3-8B, with zero grammar-first fallbacks, achieves 100\% effective coverage on SciERC, consistent with its lower residual DR (0.93\% vs.\ Llama's 0.08\%).
38	
39	%%% CF-DR Trade-off Analysis %%%
40	% exp_ids: cf_fallback_ablation_scierc (CF fallback vs full_s1 baseline)
41	
42	\paragraph{CF-DR Trade-off Analysis.}
43	\label{app:cf-dr-tradeoff}
44	
45	CF violations are the most prominent residual limitation of OntoCoDec under zero-shot decoding (9.90\% on SciERC, up to 12.02\% on Llama DocRED).
46	We treat this honestly: per-relation independent enforcement cannot eliminate CF without trading it against DR.
47	Table~\ref{tab:cf-dr-tradeoff} reports a pilot ablation in which we replace the grammar-first fallback with a CF-priority fallback that forces the entity's registered type when it conflicts with $\sigma(r)$.
48	
49	\begin{table}[t]
50	\centering
51	\small
52	\begin{tabular}{@{}l rrrr@{}}
53	\toprule
54	\textbf{Configuration} & \textbf{DR\,(\%)} & \textbf{CF\,(\%)} & \textbf{DR+CF} & \textbf{$f_{\text{gf}}$\,(\%)} \\
55	\midrule
56	Full S1 (baseline) & 0.93 & 9.90 & 10.83 & --- \\
57	CF fallback        & 14.78 & 0.04 & 14.82 & 36.64 \\
58	\midrule
59	$\Delta$ & $+$13.85 & $-$9.86 & $+$3.99 & --- \\
60	\bottomrule
61	\end{tabular}
62	\caption{CF-DR trade-off pilot on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, 551 documents; \texttt{w1\_cf\_fallback\_scierc\_pilot}). CF fallback eliminates CF but re-routes violations to DR, increasing total violations (DR+CF) by 3.99\,pp. $f_{\text{gf}}$: grammar-first fallback rate at type-bearing positions.}
63	\label{tab:cf-dr-tradeoff}
64	\end{table}
65	
66	The CF fallback variant nearly eliminates CF (9.90\%\,$\to$\,0.04\%, $-$9.86\,pp) but at the cost of a 15.9$\times$ increase in DR (0.93\%\,$\to$\,14.78\%, $+$13.85\,pp).
67	% exp_id: w1_cf_fallback_scierc_pilot: DR=0.1478, CF=0.0004, f_gf=0.3664
68	This is not a net improvement: total violations (DR+CF) rise from 10.83\% to 14.82\% ($+$3.99\,pp), so the change \emph{re-routes} violations rather than reducing them.
69	The mechanism is mechanical: each token position with conflicting masks must commit to one violation type; when the CF fallback forces the system to emit the entity's registered type even though it lies outside $\sigma(r)$, the resulting triple satisfies cross-entity consistency but violates domain/range.
70	The grammar-first fallback is triggered at 36.64\% of type-bearing positions, indicating that this conflict is structural, not a tunable hyperparameter.
71	
72	We interpret this as a fundamental tension in composable constraint systems with \emph{per-relation independent} enforcement: enforcement priority can be allocated between DR and CF but cannot independently minimize both.
73	Within this design, the current full S1 configuration sits near the Pareto frontier of the trade-off, achieving 0.93\% DR at the cost of 9.90\% CF.
74	The direction of the trade-off is consistent beyond SciERC/Qwen3-8B: across all six zero-shot configurations (3 models $\times$ 2 datasets), DR and CF are inversely associated (Spearman $\rho = -0.77$, $n{=}6$), with no setting showing both high DR and high CF simultaneously (Table~\ref{tab:cross-model}).
75	The pattern is a structural consequence of per-relation enforcement with grammar-first fallback, not a model- or dataset-specific artifact; we select SciERC/Qwen3-8B for detailed ablation because it exhibits the highest CF (9.90\%), making the trade-off most visible.
76	While the inverse association holds across all configurations, the absolute trade-off magnitude may differ in settings with higher baseline CF, such as Llama DocRED (CF = 12.02\%), where the larger CF headroom could yield proportionally larger shifts under alternative fallback priorities.
77	The CF residual is concentrated in schema ambiguity rather than enforcement failure: 63.3\% of CF violations on SciERC involve the catch-all \textsc{Generic} type (Table~\ref{tab:cf-distribution}), which competes with every content type depending on anaphoric vs.\ referential use, a distinction the per-slot decoder cannot resolve without document-level coreference.
78	
79	Two complementary paths can lower CF without re-routing it to DR.
80	(i)~\emph{Reduce the baseline conflict rate.} Composing OntoCoDec with LoRA fine-tuning on SciERC reduces CF by 88\% relative to the zero-shot setting (9.90\%\,$\to$\,1.18\%; Table~\ref{tab:composability}), because the fine-tuned model's per-slot type predictions agree more often with the entity registry, so the per-relation mask and the registry intersect more frequently.
81	% exp_id: w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval: CF=0.0118
82	The remaining 1.18\% still traces to \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X schema ambiguity, so this path is empirically validated on one dataset and one fine-tuning method but does not generalize without further evidence.
83	(ii)~\emph{Replace per-relation enforcement with global entity-level type consensus during decoding.} This is outside the scope of OntoCoDec's forward-only autoregressive design and is left to future work.
84	
85	%%% Dual-Factor Quantitative Analysis %%%
86	% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1, phase2_docred_full_s1,
87	%          llama_scierc_full_s1, llama_docred_full_s1
88	
89	\paragraph{Dual-Factor Quantitative Analysis.}
90	\label{app:dual-factor}
91	
92	Figure~\ref{fig:dual-factor-scatter} plots residual DR against the product $\bar{\kappa} \times \text{RV}_{\text{baseline}}$ for model$\times$dataset configurations.
93	For \emph{calibrated} models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B; unconstrained ET${<}$3\% on both datasets), a linear fit yields $y = 0.366x - 0.138$ with $R^2 = 0.886$ ($n{=}4$, $F(1,2) = 15.54$, $p \approx 0.058$); with only four data points (df $= 2$) and $p > 0.05$, this constitutes a descriptive characterization rather than a confirmatory statistical test.
94	The strong fit supports the dual-factor pattern from \S\ref{sec:composition}: residual DR is governed by the product of schema tightness and baseline violation rate.
95	Mistral-7B (unconstrained ET${=}$7.58\% on DocRED) deviates from this pattern: its residual DR on DocRED (33.21\%) substantially exceeds the linear prediction, confirming that when model calibration is insufficient (ET${>}$5\% on either dataset), residual DR is dominated by entity misclassification rather than constraint-search failure.
96	This motivates a principled exclusion criterion: models with unconstrained ET${>}$5\% on either dataset fall outside the regime where the tightness$\times$RV product is the primary DR driver.
97	The two DocRED points (high $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$) separate cleanly from the two SciERC points (low $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$), and within each dataset the model with higher baseline RV shows higher residual DR.
98	
99	\begin{figure}[t]
100	\centering
101	\includegraphics[width=0.75\columnwidth]{figures/dual_factor_scatter.pdf}
102	\caption{Residual DR vs.\ $\bar{\kappa} \times \text{RV}_{\text{baseline}}$ across four model$\times$dataset configurations.
103	Linear fit (calibrated models): $y = 0.366x - 0.138$, $R^2 = 0.886$; Mistral deviates due to entity misclassification.}
104	\label{fig:dual-factor-scatter}
105	\end{figure}
106	
107	%%% Dataset-Dependent F1 Impact (moved from §7) %%%
108	% exp_ids: d012_bootstrap_ci (DocRED +0.50pp p<0.001, SciERC +0.13pp p=0.58),
109	%          phase0_docred_unconstrained (RV=29.66%), phase0_scierc_unconstrained (RV=1.39%)
110	
111	\paragraph{Dataset-Dependent F1 Impact.}
112	The divergence in F1 significance between DocRED ($+$0.50\,pp, $p < 0.001$) and SciERC ($+$0.13\,pp, $p = 0.58$) traces to a single mechanism: grammar-layer elimination of out-of-vocabulary relation names.
113	DocRED's baseline RV of 29.66\% produces 5{,}189 OOV predictions counted as false positives; eliminating them yields a significant precision gain.
114	SciERC's baseline RV is only 1.39\% (24 OOV predictions), too few to produce a detectable F1 effect.
115	Llama-3.1-8B's lower baseline RV (16.03\%) yields a smaller but directionally consistent improvement ($+$0.29\,pp vs.\ $+$0.50\,pp), confirming that F1 gain magnitude is proportional to baseline OOV rate.
116	% exp_ids: phase0_docred_unconstrained, phase0_scierc_unconstrained
117	% exp_ids: llama_docred_unconstrained (RV=16.03%), llama_docred_full_s1 (R-F1 delta=+0.29pp)
118	
119	%%% Paragraph 1: Low F1 Practical Significance %%%
120	% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1 (R-F1=8.36%), phase2_docred_full_s1 (R-F1=8.23%),
121	%          phase0_scierc_unconstrained (DR=15.37%), phase2_docred_unconstrained (DR=18.46%)
122	
123	\paragraph{Practical Significance of Zero-Shot F1.}
124	Our reported relation F1 of approximately 8\% on both SciERC and DocRED reflects the inherent difficulty of zero-shot closed IE, where the model receives no task-specific training examples.
125	For reference, supervised state-of-the-art systems on SciERC achieve approximately 49--53\% relation F1 with full training data~\citep{zhong2021frustratingly,ye2022packed}.
126	Constraint enforcement operates largely independently of the extraction model's intrinsic capability: it restricts the output space to ontologically valid triples regardless of the underlying model's accuracy.
127	When applied to fine-tuned models that reach competitive F1 levels, the same constraints remain necessary: Phase~0 analysis confirms that even well-prompted models exhibit non-trivial violation rates (15.37\% DR on SciERC, 18.46\% on DocRED).
128	% exp_ids: phase0_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_docred_unconstrained
129	In our evaluation, F1 serves as a \emph{control variable} verifying that constraint enforcement does not degrade extraction quality, not as an optimization target.
130	The contribution of this work is the constraint enforcement method itself; the zero-shot setting isolates its effect from confounds introduced by task-specific fine-tuning.
131	
132	%%% Paragraph 4: Decoding-Time vs. Post-Hoc Enforcement %%%
133	% exp_ids: posthoc_filtering_baseline, phase2_scierc_full_s1 (R-F1=8.36%),
134	%          phase2_docred_full_s1 (R-F1=8.23%, ET=0%)
135	
136	\paragraph{Decoding-Time vs.\ Post-Hoc Enforcement.}
137	Post-hoc filtering (generating triples without constraints, then removing schema-violating predictions) yields higher precision and consequently higher F1 than OntoCoDec on both datasets (SciERC 8.63 vs.\ 8.36; DocRED 9.61 vs.\ 8.23).
138	% posthoc: SciERC F1=8.63, DocRED F1=9.61; OntoCoDec: SciERC R-F1=8.36, DocRED R-F1=8.23
139	However, this precision gain comes at substantial cost.

% Appendix B — Extended Discussion
% Contains discussion paragraphs moved from the main text during compression.

\section{Extended Discussion}\label{app:discussion}

%%% CF Dual Mechanism %%%
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1, llama_scierc_full_s1, llama_docred_full_s1

\paragraph{CF Dual Mechanism.}
CF violations arise from two distinct mechanisms:
(1)~\emph{Registry override}: the semantic constraint forces a domain-compatible type that conflicts with the entity's previously registered type.
The entity appears in multiple relations with different type requirements, and the per-relation mask selects the locally valid type without consulting prior assignments.
(2)~\emph{Grammar-first fallback} (\S\ref{sec:interaction}): when the semantic mask conflicts with all grammar-valid tokens, the semantic layer is dropped entirely, allowing the grammar layer to generate any structurally valid type, which may differ from the entity's registered type.

These mechanisms have sharply different model profiles.
Qwen3-8B triggers zero grammar-first fallbacks across all experiments, attributing 100\% of its CF violations to registry override.
Llama-3.1-8B, by contrast, triggers 5{,}882 fallbacks on SciERC (10.7 per document) and 57{,}825 on DocRED (63.8 per document), making grammar-first fallback the dominant CF source.
This asymmetry is consistent with the cross-model CF gap: Qwen achieves CF\,=\,2.57\% on DocRED vs.\ Llama's 12.02\%, despite both using identical constraint configurations.
The difference traces to Llama's less calibrated type predictions, which more frequently conflict with the semantic mask's valid set, triggering fallback.

%%% Fallback Behavior and Effective Coverage %%%
% exp_ids: cf_fallback_ablation_scierc (final data)

\paragraph{Fallback Behavior and Effective Coverage.}
\label{app:fallback-coverage}
The two-layer architecture produces two distinct fallback mechanisms with different semantic consequences.
\emph{Grammar-first fallback} (36.6\% of type-bearing positions on SciERC) occurs when $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$: the semantic layer deactivates as a safety valve, preserving structural validity at the cost of potential type violations. These events account for the residual DR that persists after constraint enforcement.
\emph{Registry-consistent fallback} (4.5\%) occurs when the entity's registered type conflicts with domain/range constraints; the system defaults to the registered type for cross-triple consistency.
Together, these mechanisms produce the characteristic profile of composable constraint systems: residual DR traces to grammar-first fallback events, while CF violations arise from registry override events where per-relation enforcement assigns conflicting types.

We define \emph{effective semantic constraint coverage} as $1 - f_{\text{gf}}$, where $f_{\text{gf}}$ is the grammar-first fallback rate.
On SciERC, Llama-3.1-8B shows $f_{\text{gf}} = 36.6\%$ (6{,}237 of 17{,}024 mask calls), yielding 63.4\% effective coverage.
On DocRED, by contrast, Qwen3-8B shows $f_{\text{gf}} = 0.08\%$ (46 of 54{,}859), yielding 99.9\% coverage.
The large discrepancy is primarily a tokenization artifact: SciERC entity types are multi-token (e.g., \textsc{OtherScientificTerm}, averaging 2.87 mask calls per type field), and continuation tokens necessarily conflict with the semantic mask, inflating the per-mask-call fallback rate.
DocRED types (\textsc{PER}, \textsc{ORG}, \textsc{LOC}, \textsc{TIME}, \textsc{NUM}, \textsc{MISC}) are all single-token, eliminating this inflation.
This metric directly quantifies the enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:interaction}): it measures the fraction of decoding steps where both constraint layers are jointly active, providing a fine-grained view beyond aggregate violation rates.
Qwen3-8B, with zero grammar-first fallbacks, achieves 100\% effective coverage on SciERC, consistent with its lower residual DR (0.93\% vs.\ Llama's 0.08\%).

%%% CF-DR Trade-off Analysis %%%
% exp_ids: cf_fallback_ablation_scierc (CF fallback vs full_s1 baseline)

\paragraph{CF-DR Trade-off Analysis.}
\label{app:cf-dr-tradeoff}

CF violations are the most prominent residual limitation of OntoCoDec under zero-shot decoding (9.90\% on SciERC, up to 12.02\% on Llama DocRED).
We treat this honestly: per-relation independent enforcement cannot eliminate CF without trading it against DR.
Table~\ref{tab:cf-dr-tradeoff} reports a pilot ablation in which we replace the grammar-first fallback with a CF-priority fallback that forces the entity's registered type when it conflicts with $\sigma(r)$.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}l rrrr@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Configuration} & \textbf{DR\,(\%)} & \textbf{CF\,(\%)} & \textbf{DR+CF} & \textbf{$f_{\text{gf}}$\,(\%)} \\
\midrule
Full S1 (baseline) & 0.93 & 9.90 & 10.83 & --- \\
CF fallback        & 14.78 & 0.04 & 14.82 & 36.64 \\
\midrule
$\Delta$ & $+$13.85 & $-$9.86 & $+$3.99 & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{CF-DR trade-off pilot on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, 551 documents; \texttt{w1\_cf\_fallback\_scierc\_pilot}). CF fallback eliminates CF but re-routes violations to DR, increasing total violations (DR+CF) by 3.99\,pp. $f_{\text{gf}}$: grammar-first fallback rate at type-bearing positions.}
\label{tab:cf-dr-tradeoff}
\end{table}

The CF fallback variant nearly eliminates CF (9.90\%\,$\to$\,0.04\%, $-$9.86\,pp) but at the cost of a 15.9$\times$ increase in DR (0.93\%\,$\to$\,14.78\%, $+$13.85\,pp).
% exp_id: w1_cf_fallback_scierc_pilot: DR=0.1478, CF=0.0004, f_gf=0.3664
This is not a net improvement: total violations (DR+CF) rise from 10.83\% to 14.82\% ($+$3.99\,pp), so the change \emph{re-routes} violations rather than reducing them.
The mechanism is mechanical: each token position with conflicting masks must commit to one violation type; when the CF fallback forces the system to emit the entity's registered type even though it lies outside $\sigma(r)$, the resulting triple satisfies cross-entity consistency but violates domain/range.
The grammar-first fallback is triggered at 36.64\% of type-bearing positions, indicating that this conflict is structural, not a tunable hyperparameter.

We interpret this as a fundamental tension in composable constraint systems with \emph{per-relation independent} enforcement: enforcement priority can be allocated between DR and CF but cannot independently minimize both.
Within this design, the current full S1 configuration sits near the Pareto frontier of the trade-off, achieving 0.93\% DR at the cost of 9.90\% CF.
The direction of the trade-off is consistent beyond SciERC/Qwen3-8B: across all six zero-shot configurations (3 models $\times$ 2 datasets), DR and CF are inversely associated (Spearman $\rho = -0.77$, $n{=}6$), with no setting showing both high DR and high CF simultaneously (Table~\ref{tab:cross-model}).
The pattern is a structural consequence of per-relation enforcement with grammar-first fallback, not a model- or dataset-specific artifact; we select SciERC/Qwen3-8B for detailed ablation because it exhibits the highest CF (9.90\%), making the trade-off most visible.
While the inverse association holds across all configurations, the absolute trade-off magnitude may differ in settings with higher baseline CF, such as Llama DocRED (CF = 12.02\%), where the larger CF headroom could yield proportionally larger shifts under alternative fallback priorities.
The CF residual is concentrated in schema ambiguity rather than enforcement failure: 63.3\% of CF violations on SciERC involve the catch-all \textsc{Generic} type (Table~\ref{tab:cf-distribution}), which competes with every content type depending on anaphoric vs.\ referential use, a distinction the per-slot decoder cannot resolve without document-level coreference.

Two complementary paths can lower CF without re-routing it to DR.
(i)~\emph{Reduce the baseline conflict rate.} Composing OntoCoDec with LoRA fine-tuning on SciERC reduces CF by 88\% relative to the zero-shot setting (9.90\%\,$\to$\,1.18\%; Table~\ref{tab:composability}), because the fine-tuned model's per-slot type predictions agree more often with the entity registry, so the per-relation mask and the registry intersect more frequently.
% exp_id: w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval: CF=0.0118
The remaining 1.18\% still traces to \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X schema ambiguity, so this path is empirically validated on one dataset and one fine-tuning method but does not generalize without further evidence.
(ii)~\emph{Replace per-relation enforcement with global entity-level type consensus during decoding.} This is outside the scope of OntoCoDec's forward-only autoregressive design and is left to future work.

\paragraph{Dual-Factor Quantitative Analysis.}
\label{app:dual-factor}

Figure~\ref{fig:dual-factor-scatter} plots residual DR against the product $\bar{\kappa} \times \text{RV}_{\text{baseline}}$ for model$\times$dataset configurations.
For \emph{calibrated} models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B; unconstrained ET${<}$3\% on both datasets), a linear fit yields $y = 0.366x - 0.138$ with $R^2 = 0.886$ ($n{=}4$, $F(1,2) = 15.54$, $p \approx 0.058$); with only four data points (df $= 2$) and $p > 0.05$, this constitutes a descriptive characterization rather than a confirmatory statistical test.
The strong fit supports the dual-factor pattern from \S\ref{sec:composition}: residual DR is governed by the product of schema tightness and baseline violation rate.
Mistral-7B (unconstrained ET${=}$7.58\% on DocRED) deviates from this pattern: its residual DR on DocRED (33.21\%) substantially exceeds the linear prediction, confirming that when model calibration is insufficient (ET${>}$5\% on either dataset), residual DR is dominated by entity misclassification rather than constraint-search failure.
This motivates a principled exclusion criterion: models with unconstrained ET${>}$5\% on either dataset fall outside the regime where the tightness$\times$RV product is the primary DR driver.
The two DocRED points (high $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$) separate cleanly from the two SciERC points (low $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$), and within each dataset the model with higher baseline RV shows higher residual DR.

\paragraph{Dataset-Dependent F1 Impact.}
The divergence in F1 significance between DocRED ($+$0.50\,pp, $p < 0.001$) and SciERC ($+$0.13\,pp, $p = 0.58$) traces to a single mechanism: grammar-layer elimination of out-of-vocabulary relation names.
DocRED's baseline RV of 29.66\% produces 5{,}189 OOV predictions counted as false positives; eliminating them yields a significant precision gain.
SciERC's baseline RV is only 1.39\% (24 OOV predictions), too few to produce a detectable F1 effect.
Llama-3.1-8B's lower baseline RV (16.03\%) yields a smaller but directionally consistent improvement ($+$0.29\,pp vs.\ $+$0.50\,pp), confirming that F1 gain magnitude is proportional to baseline OOV rate.

%%% Paragraph 1: Low F1 Practical Significance %%%
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1 (R-F1=8.36%), phase2_docred_full_s1 (R-F1=8.23%),
%          phase0_scierc_unconstrained (DR=15.37%), phase2_docred_unconstrained (DR=18.46%)

\paragraph{Practical Significance of Zero-Shot F1.}
Our reported relation F1 of approximately 8\% on both SciERC and DocRED reflects the inherent difficulty of zero-shot closed IE, where the model receives no task-specific training examples.
For reference, supervised state-of-the-art systems on SciERC achieve approximately 49--53\% relation F1 with full training data~\citep{zhong2021frustratingly,ye2022packed}.
Constraint enforcement operates largely independently of the extraction model's intrinsic capability: it restricts the output space to ontologically valid triples regardless of the underlying model's accuracy.
When applied to fine-tuned models that reach competitive F1 levels, the same constraints remain necessary: Phase~0 analysis confirms that even well-prompted models exhibit non-trivial violation rates (15.37\% DR on SciERC, 18.46\% on DocRED).
% exp_ids: phase0_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_docred_unconstrained
In our evaluation, F1 serves as a \emph{control variable} verifying that constraint enforcement does not degrade extraction quality, not as an optimization target.
The contribution of this work is the constraint enforcement method itself; the zero-shot setting isolates its effect from confounds introduced by task-specific fine-tuning.

%%% Paragraph 4: Decoding-Time vs. Post-Hoc Enforcement %%%
% exp_ids: posthoc_filtering_baseline, phase2_scierc_full_s1 (R-F1=8.36%),
%          phase2_docred_full_s1 (R-F1=8.23%, ET=0%)

\paragraph{Decoding-Time vs.\ Post-Hoc Enforcement.}
Post-hoc filtering (generating triples without constraints, then removing schema-violating predictions) yields higher precision and consequently higher F1 than OntoCoDec on both datasets (SciERC 8.63 vs.\ 8.36; DocRED 9.61 vs.\ 8.23).
% posthoc: SciERC F1=8.63, DocRED F1=9.61; OntoCoDec: SciERC R-F1=8.36, DocRED R-F1=8.23
However, this precision gain comes at substantial cost.
On DocRED, post-hoc filtering discards 48.1\% of all predicted triples, including 127 true positives (11.2\% of correct predictions), reducing recall from 9.46\% to 8.40\%.
% posthoc_docred: rejection=48.1%, tp_lost=127/1137, R: 9.46→8.40
Entity type violations remain unresolved (ET\,=\,2.47\% vs.\ OntoCoDec's 0\%), as filtering targets only domain/range and vocabulary violations.
% posthoc_docred: ET_residual=2.47%; phase2_docred_full_s1: ET=0%
OntoCoDec's decoding-time approach avoids this information loss by guiding generation toward compliant outputs rather than discarding non-compliant ones, preserving both recall and entity type validity.
The two strategies are complementary: post-hoc filtering can serve as an additional safety net for residual violations that decoding-time enforcement does not fully resolve.

\paragraph{Residual DR Error Analysis.}
\label{app:residual-dr-analysis}

Across all fine-tuned settings (2 models $\times$ 2 datasets $\times$ full S1), only 36 domain/range violations remain.
Manual inspection reveals four root causes:

\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item \emph{Entity type errors} (39\%): the LLM assigns an incorrect entity type (e.g., labeling a geographic entity as \textsc{LOC} when the gold standard requires \textsc{MISC}), causing the semantic mask to permit a domain/range-incompatible relation.
\item \emph{Schema coverage gaps} (33\%): the frequency-based constraint table, constructed from training-set co-occurrence statistics, does not cover long-tail type pairs that are ontologically valid but rare. These violations are irreducible by decoding-time constraints alone.
\item \emph{Incorrect relation selection} (17\%): the model selects a semantically inappropriate relation whose domain/range constraints are incompatible with the correctly typed entities.
\item \emph{Direction reversal} (11\%): the model assigns the correct relation but inverts head/tail roles, placing entities in positions that violate the relation's asymmetric domain/range specification.
\end{enumerate}

Two dataset-specific patterns emerge.
Outside Llama DocRED, all residual violations (3 of 36, spanning Llama SciERC and Qwen DocRED) trace exclusively to schema coverage gaps: the model's entity typing is accurate, and the constraint system has reached its theoretical ceiling given the frequency-based constraint table.
On DocRED, Llama-3.1-8B contributes 33 of 36 residual violations (92\%), with entity type errors as the dominant cause (14/33, 42\%).
This asymmetry reflects Llama's weaker fine-tuned entity typing on DocRED's larger ontology (96 relations, 7 entity types) compared to Qwen, which achieves near-zero residual.
The implication is twofold: (i)~the irreducible floor from schema gaps is small ($\sim$3 violations across 4 settings), confirming that the constraint system operates near its theoretical optimum; (ii)~residual violations from entity typing errors are addressable through stronger base models or improved entity typing modules, without modifying the constraint architecture.

%%% Fuzzy Relation Matching %%%

\paragraph{Relation Matching Protocol.}
\label{app:fuzzy-matching}
Relation F1 evaluation uses fuzzy normalization to handle model-specific formatting variants (e.g., underscores vs.\ spaces, abbreviations).
A predicted relation $r_p$ matches gold relation $r_g$ if: (1)~exact string match after case-insensitive normalization, or (2)~token overlap $>$80\% \emph{and} edit distance $\leq 2$.
This protocol affects primarily Mistral, which produces underscore-separated variants (e.g., ``head\_of\_government'' for ``head of government'').
On Mistral DocRED, fuzzy matching contributes 98 additional TPs ($+$0.84\,pp R-F1; strict R-F1\,=\,3.50\% vs.\ fuzzy 4.34\%).
For Qwen and Llama under grammar constraints, the grammar layer enforces exact relation names, making fuzzy matching irrelevant (0 additional matches).
All F1 figures in the main text use fuzzy normalization consistently across all models and conditions.

\paragraph{WikiEvents Dataset Details.}
\label{app:wikievents}
WikiEvents~\cite{li2021document} is a document-level event argument extraction benchmark grounded in the DARPA KAIROS ontology.
It defines 56 event types, 80 argument roles, and 27 entity types, with 245 (event\_type, role)$\to$allowed\_entity\_types constraints.
The grammar layer targets EV (event vocabulary), RoV (role vocabulary), and ET; the semantic layer enforces AC (argument constraint) via role-conditioned masking, analogous to RE domain/range enforcement.

4	OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is designed to be decoding-strategy agnostic.

8	\paragraph{Implementation challenges.}
9	Two stateful components require adaptation for beam search.
10	(1)~The grammar layer (XGrammar) maintains an internal \texttt{GrammarMatcher} state that tracks the generated token sequence; beam reordering invalidates this state because beams are permuted across steps.
11	Our solution instantiates a fresh \texttt{GrammarMatcher} per beam per step and replays the beam's current token sequence through XGrammar's stateless accept API (64 lines of code).
12	(2)~The semantic layer's \texttt{TypeConstraintProcessor} accumulates entity and relation registries that assume a single generation path.
13	Our solution isolates state per beam by calling \texttt{detect()} on the full partial output at each step, reconstructing all entity/relation state from scratch for each beam independently (61 lines of code).
14	Both adaptations add ${\sim}125$ lines total without modifying the existing greedy/sampling logic.

\section{Beam Search Compatibility}
\label{app:beam-search}

OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is designed to be decoding-strategy agnostic.
The main experiments (\S\ref{sec:experiments}) use greedy decoding; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling} validates nucleus sampling.
Here we verify compatibility with beam search, completing coverage of the three standard decoding strategies.

\paragraph{Implementation challenges.}
Two stateful components require adaptation for beam search.
(1)~The grammar layer (XGrammar) maintains an internal \texttt{GrammarMatcher} state that tracks the generated token sequence; beam reordering invalidates this state because beams are permuted across steps.
Our solution instantiates a fresh \texttt{GrammarMatcher} per beam per step and replays the beam's current token sequence through XGrammar's stateless accept API (64 lines of code).
(2)~The semantic layer's \texttt{TypeConstraintProcessor} accumulates entity and relation registries that assume a single generation path.
Our solution isolates state per beam by calling \texttt{detect()} on the full partial output at each step, reconstructing all entity/relation state from scratch for each beam independently (61 lines of code).
Both adaptations add ${\sim}125$ lines total without modifying the existing greedy/sampling logic.

\paragraph{Results.}
Table~\ref{tab:beam-search} compares beam search ($k{=}4$, \texttt{early\_stopping=True}) against greedy decoding under full S1 constraints across six model-dataset combinations.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Beam search ($k{=}4$) vs.\ greedy decoding under full S1 constraints.
SciERC evaluated on full test set (551 documents); DocRED evaluated on matched 50-document subsets (same documents for greedy and beam).
ET = entity type, RV = relation vocabulary, DR = domain/range, CF = cross-field consistency violation rates (\%); F1 $\times$ 100.}
\label{tab:beam-search}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Model / Dataset} & \textbf{Decoding} & ET & RV & DR$\,\downarrow$ & CF$\,\downarrow$ & E-F1$\,\uparrow$ & R-F1$\,\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Qwen3-8B / SciERC (551)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 0.93 & 9.90 & 30.98 & 8.36 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.53} & 32.00 & 8.56 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Qwen3-8B / DocRED (50)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 8.69 & 2.08 & 59.08 & 8.33 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.55} & 58.64 & 9.37 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Llama-3.1-8B / SciERC (551)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 0.08 & 6.56 & 23.49 & 2.54 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.93} & 25.04 & 3.33 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Llama-3.1-8B / DocRED (50)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 1.58 & 6.85 & 55.35 & 6.12 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.94} & 55.62 & 9.47 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Mistral-7B / SciERC (551)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 13.40 & 1.27 & 27.46 & 3.67 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & 13.79 & \textbf{0.57} & 26.66 & 4.37 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Mistral-7B / DocRED (50)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 28.37 & 0.34 & 51.60 & 4.19 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{21.37} & \textbf{0.19} & 51.78 & 5.70 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Discussion.}
For calibrated models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B), beam search achieves DR=0\% across all four model-dataset combinations (both SciERC with 7 entity types, 551 documents, and DocRED with 96 relation types, 50 documents), regardless of schema complexity.
On SciERC, beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (0.93\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (0.08\%\,$\to$\,0\%), and substantially reduces CF (Qwen: 9.90\%\,$\to$\,0.53\%; Llama: 6.56\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).
On DocRED (matched 50-document subsets), beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (8.69\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (1.58\%\,$\to$\,0\%), with CF reductions of 74\% and 86\% respectively.
Llama DocRED shows the largest R-F1 gain ($+$3.4\,pp), consistent with beam search recovering valid type assignments that greedy decoding missed due to constraint fallback.
The CF reduction is an indirect effect: beam search reduces constraint-fallback frequency by exploring alternative token sequences that satisfy both grammar and semantic masks simultaneously, avoiding the fallback-to-grammar path that produces cross-field inconsistencies under greedy decoding.

Mistral-7B-v0.3 constitutes a boundary condition on both datasets.
On SciERC (7 entity types), beam search does not reduce DR (13.4\%\,$\to$\,13.8\%), though CF drops by 55\% relative (1.27\%\,$\to$\,0.57\%) and R-F1 improves by $+$0.7\,pp; the unchanged DR confirms that all residual violations stem from entity type misclassification, not constraint-search failure.
On DocRED (96 relation types), beam search reduces DR by 25\% relative (28.4\%\,$\to$\,21.4\%): the more complex schema introduces constraint-search failures that beam exploration resolves, but the entity misclassification component remains.
This contrast reveals that beam search resolves constraint-search failure (where greedy decoding encounters $G(t) \cap S(t) = \emptyset$ conflicts) but cannot overcome fundamental model calibration limitations in entity typing.

\paragraph{Beam width ablation.}
Table~\ref{tab:beam-ablation} varies beam width $k \in \{1,2,4,8\}$ on Qwen3-8B / SciERC (551 documents) under full S1 constraints.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Effect of beam width on constraint satisfaction and extraction quality (Qwen3-8B, SciERC, 551 documents, full S1 constraints). $k{=}1$ corresponds to greedy decoding.}
\label{tab:beam-ablation}
\begin{tabular}{@{}rcccc@{}}
\toprule
$k$ & DR$\,\downarrow$ & CF$\,\downarrow$ & E-F1$\,\uparrow$ & R-F1$\,\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
1 (greedy) & 0.93 & 9.90 & 30.98 & 8.36 \\
2          & 0.35 & 4.12 & 31.54 & \textbf{8.75} \\
4          & \textbf{0}    & 0.53 & 32.00 & 8.56 \\
8          & \textbf{0}    & \textbf{0.08} & \textbf{32.18} & 8.39 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

DR elimination at $k{\geq}4$ confirms that constraint-search failure is resolved with moderate exploration width.
CF continues to decrease with larger beam (0.08\% at $k{=}8$, only 2 residual violations), while entity extraction quality improves monotonically.
$k{=}4$ represents the optimal cost-effectiveness trade-off: it eliminates all DR violations at roughly half the compute cost of $k{=}8$.

\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
Under greedy decoding, the fine-tuned Qwen3-8B (LoRA, SciERC) with full S1 constraints already achieves DR=0\% but retains CF=1.18\% (21 cross-field violations across 551 documents), with E-F1=67.05 and R-F1=43.77.
Adding beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all residual CF violations (1.18\%\,$\to$\,0\%), yielding zero violations across all four metrics (ET=0\%, RV=0\%, DR=0\%, CF=0\%) while preserving extraction quality (E-F1=66.88, R-F1=44.23; changes within $\pm$0.5\,pp).
Llama-3.1-8B (LoRA, SciERC) with full S1 constraints and beam search ($k{=}4$) likewise achieves zero violations across all four metrics (ET=0\%, RV=0\%, DR=0\%, CF=0\%) with R-F1=46.11; the zero-violation result thus generalizes across calibrated model families.
% exp_id: q1_llama_ft_beam_scierc
The three constraint mechanisms (grammar masking, semantic domain-range filtering, and beam exploration) are thus fully composable: each addresses a distinct violation source without interfering with the others or degrading task performance.

Beam search on DocRED introduces a modest increase in parse failures (3/50, 6\%) compared to greedy (1.1\%), as longer beam-generated sequences occasionally produce malformed JSON in complex documents.
Wall-clock overhead is modest; \texttt{early\_stopping} terminates generation once all beams produce a complete sequence, limiting the additional compute to partial-sequence exploration rather than full-length replication.
Combined with the sampling robustness results (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling}), these findings confirm that OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is compatible with greedy, sampling, and beam search decoding without modification to the core constraint logic.

We also explored a type-consensus constraint that forces identical entity types across all relations within a document.
However, CF violations occur precisely where the consensus type conflicts with domain-range constraints, creating a fundamental CF$\leftrightarrow$DR trade-off.
With DR-aware enforcement (skipping consensus when it would violate domain-range), the layer becomes a no-op (100\% skip rate on 551 SciERC documents and 50 DocRED documents).
This confirms that beam search resolves the CF$\leftrightarrow$DR tension through a fundamentally different mechanism: token-level exploration of paths satisfying both constraints simultaneously.

8	\label{sec:wikievents}
9	
10	To test generality beyond RE, we apply OntoCoDec to event extraction (EE) on WikiEvents~\cite{li2021document} (56 event types, 80 argument roles, 27 entity types, 245 role$\to$type constraints; Appendix~\ref{app:wikievents}).
11	The framework requires no modification: grammar compiles event/role vocabularies into a CFG; the semantic layer enforces role-conditioned type constraints via the same registry.
12	Violations extend to Event Vocabulary (EV), Role Vocabulary (RoV), and Argument Constraint (AC, analogous to DR).

55	\paragraph{Results.}
56	Unconstrained generation produces extreme vocabulary violations (EV+RoV exceeding 85\% combined; Table~\ref{tab:wikievents}), and all models yield entity F1\,=\,0 because the parser cannot identify well-formed mentions in off-schema output.
57	Full S1 eliminates EV and RoV across all three models ($\to$\,0\%), which validates tokenizer-agnostic design across byte-level BPE (Qwen, Llama) and SentencePiece (Mistral).
58	Grammar-only ablation isolates each layer: grammar eliminates EV ($\to$\,0\%) but leaves RoV at 64--77\% because the CFG cannot constrain 80 argument roles conditioned on event context; AC rises from near-zero to 8--14\%, the same latent-violation surfacing pattern observed in DocRED (\S\ref{sec:docred-results}).
59	Full S1 then drives RoV to 0\%, which demonstrates layer complementarity.
60	Residual AC (1.3--3.8\%) traces to confusion between semantically similar entity types (e.g., SID vs.\ SEN) where grammar-first fallback permits the incorrect type; CF rises to 15--21\%, consistent with the per-slot enforcement trade-off in RE.
61	
62	Post-hoc filtering is impractical for EE: it retains only 23/5{,}467 arguments for Qwen (99.6\% discarded), 3/5{,}053 for Llama, and 0/6{,}034 for Mistral, because unconstrained models generate generic role names rather than ontology-specific ones.
63	Unlike RE, where constraints are F1-neutral, EE shows measurable gains: entity F1 rises from 0\% to 11.7--17.6\% and trigger F1 increases by $+$1.5--1.8\,pp, because grammar enforcement produces schema-valid JSON that the parser can process.

\subsection{Cross-Task Validation: Event Extraction}
\label{sec:wikievents}

To test generality beyond RE, we apply OntoCoDec to event extraction (EE) on WikiEvents~\cite{li2021document} (56 event types, 80 argument roles, 27 entity types, 245 role$\to$type constraints; Appendix~\ref{app:wikievents}).
The framework requires no modification: grammar compiles event/role vocabularies into a CFG; the semantic layer enforces role-conditioned type constraints via the same registry.
Violations extend to Event Vocabulary (EV), Role Vocabulary (RoV), and Argument Constraint (AC, analogous to DR).
